title: Mise en Place in Teaching Foundational Reading and Spelling
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: This guest post from Jennifer Newman, a speech-language therapist and reading specialist, argues that Diane McGuinness's Linguistic Phonics approach provides a more coherent, efficient framework for teaching foundational reading and spelling than popular US curricula — because it applies the culinary principle of 'mise en place' (preparing all ingredients and tools before cooking) to the structure of reading instruction itself. McGuinness's key insight is that the English alphabetic code should be taught in the direction it was written: from sounds to spellings rather than from graphemes to phonemes, anchored in a finite set of roughly 40 phonemes. This phoneme-first orientation eliminates the need for syllable types, decoding rules, irregular 'heart words,' and articulatory gesture instruction — reducing cognitive load and freeing teachers to focus on responsive teaching. Common US curricula built on visual-phonics logic (UFLI, Fundations, Orton-Gillingham methods) use the same instructional activities but organized in an opposite framework, creating confusion about the code's reversible logic and leading to compensatory strategies like whole-word guessing.
points: Diane McGuinness's Linguistic Phonics applies the culinary principle of mise en place — prepare and organize ingredients before cooking — to reading instruction: how the alphabetic code is organized before teaching begins fundamentally shapes efficiency and coherence.

McGuinness argues the English code should be taught phoneme-first (40 sounds to multiple spellings and back), not grapheme-first (letter by letter); this distinction is frequently misunderstood even among phonics advocates.

Popular US phonics curricula (UFLI, Fundations, Orton-Gillingham-based methods) use visual-phonics logic — organizing instruction around graphemes rather than phonemes — losing the reversible logic of the code and forcing unnecessary complexity onto teachers and students.

Linguistic Phonics eliminates the need for syllable types, decoding rules, irregular 'heart words,' articulatory gesture instruction, and separate phonemic awareness exercises — all of which are byproducts of grapheme-first instruction.

When children are not shown that English is a reversible code, they develop wrong logic about how the writing system works, leading to compensatory strategies like letter-name decoding, whole-word visual memorization, and guessing that initiate a damaging cycle.
quotes: when teaching a complex written code like English, how we prepare, measure, and organize the ingredients before instruction begins influences not only how efficiently students acquire foundational skills but also the time and energy teachers have available to help students become thoughtful, proficient readers and writers.

McGuinness argues we need to take great care in how we present the code. Her point is that failing to attend to mise en place in English reading instruction creates a trap that can lead to bad habits, slower progress, frustration, and poor outcomes.
If the code is taught in the direction in which it was written, 40 sounds to multiple spelling alternatives and back again, the code nature of the writing system remains intact.
The critical difference lies not in the instructional activities themselves, but in the organizational framework that gives those activities meaning.
When graphemes drive foundational instruction, the system loses its boundaries, and there is no way to get back to the phonemes it was created to represent.

When adults fail to ‘make sense’ of what they are trying to teach, children will struggle to impose some kind of logic on how a writing system works. More often than not, this will be the wrong logic.

Compensatory strategies such as letter-name decoding, looking at the pictures, whole-word visual memorization, and guessing are the main outcomes when children are left to their own devices or are required to employ the propositional logic of if then with rules.
